claim: A sole proprietorship needs no separate registration to exist: it is created the moment one person starts trading in their own name or a trade name. Founders usually still get a current bank account (needs Udyam/GST/Shop Act as proof of business) and a GST registration if turnover crosses the threshold. Total setup cost is typically ₹1,000-5,000 and takes 3-7 days for the supporting registrations, but there is no separate 'exit': the business just stops when the owner stops, and any business debt is personal debt.

claim: A partnership firm needs at least two partners and a partnership deed; registering it with the Registrar of Firms is optional but cheap (stamp duty on the deed roughly ₹200-1,000 plus a registrar fee of ₹300-2,000 depending on the state, so ₹1,000-5,000 all-in with a CA drafting the deed) and usually takes 1-3 weeks once documents are in. Nothing forces registration, and many small partnerships never do it.

claim: An unregistered partnership firm can still operate, invoice and pay tax, but under section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act it cannot sue a third party or another partner to enforce a contract, and a partner cannot sue the firm or co-partners over firm matters. Founders find this out only when a customer or a falling-out partner refuses to pay and a lawyer explains the firm has no standing to claim it in court.

claim: An LLP needs at least two designated partners (at least one resident in India), each with a DSC and DIN/DPIN, and is incorporated through the FiLLiP form. End-to-end it typically takes 7-15 working days and costs roughly ₹5,000-12,000 all-in for a small LLP once professional fees are included, mainly because LLP incorporation fees scale with contribution amount and DSC/professional charges dominate at small scale. It suits two or more founders who want limited liability without private-limited-style compliance and investor-facing structure.

claim: An LLP that does nothing after incorporation still owes two annual filings regardless of turnover: Form 11 (annual return of partners) by 30 May and Form 8 (statement of account and solvency) around 30 October. Skipping them does not close the LLP; it accumulates additional fees and eventually blocks other MCA filings until cleared.

claim: A One Person Company (OPC) lets a single Indian-resident individual hold 100% ownership with limited liability; it needs one shareholder, one mandatory nominee (also an Indian citizen), and at least one director resident in India for 182+ days a year. Registration costs roughly ₹10,000-25,000 all-in (government fee, DSC ₹2,000-3,000, state stamp duty, professional fee ₹5,000-15,000) and takes about 5-8 working days once documents are ready. The old rule forcing mandatory conversion to a private limited company above ₹50 lakh paid-up capital or ₹2 crore turnover was removed in 2021; conversion is now voluntary.

claim: A private limited company needs a minimum of two shareholders and two directors (same people can be both), can have up to 200 shareholders, and is the entity most B2B customers, investors and payment processors expect. It is also the most expensive to keep alive when idle: unlike a sole proprietorship or an unregistered partnership, it cannot simply be abandoned without cost or consequence.

claim: Every proposed director needs a Class 3 Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) before SPICe+ can be filed, bought from a licensed certifying authority for roughly ₹1,000-2,000 per director including the USB token, valid for 1-3 years depending on what is purchased. A DSC needs a live photo/video verification step, which is the most common place a first-time founder gets stuck.

claim: Director Identification Numbers (DIN) for new directors are allotted directly through SPICe+ Part B at incorporation, so a first-time founder does not need a separate DIR-3 application. A director who is added later, after the company already exists, does need a standalone DIR-3 filing with its own DSC and verification step, which is slower than getting a DIN at incorporation.

claim: SPICe+ Part A (name reservation) costs ₹1,000 and, once approved, reserves the name for 20 days from approval; that can be extended up to 60 days by paying an extra fee. A founder who reserves a name and then sits on it past the window has to pay again and re-run the approval.

claim: Each SPICe+ Part A submission allows up to two proposed names, with at least one mandatory. If the Central Registration Centre (CRC) marks the application 'resubmission required' instead of outright rejecting it, the founder must resubmit within roughly 15 days of that flag using the same ₹1,000 fee already paid; a hard rejection means starting over and paying again.

claim: MCA charges zero registration fee on SPICe+ Part B for a company whose authorised share capital is up to ₹15 lakh; above that threshold, incremental government fees kick in and scale with capital. Founders are advised to start with a low authorised capital (e.g. ₹1 lakh or ₹10 lakh) and raise it later by a separate filing, rather than pay incorporation fees on a large capital they do not need yet.

A founder who picks a registered-office state without checking this can be surprised by a bill several times higher than expected.

claim: AGILE-PRO-S is filed alongside SPICe+ Part B and bundles several registrations into one incorporation: GSTIN (only if the registered office matches the correspondence address given), EPFO and ESIC numbers (issued automatically for every company regardless of employee count), profession tax registration (only in Karnataka, Maharashtra and West Bengal), an option to open a current bank account with a partner bank, and Shops & Establishment registration (only for Mumbai or Delhi registered offices). None of these open automatically outside their stated conditions, which is why founders elsewhere still end up doing GST or bank KYC by hand later.

claim: SPICe+ Part A / RUN names get rejected in a handful of recurring buckets under the Companies (Incorporation) Rules 2014: too close to an existing company/LLP name once suffixes and spelling variants are ignored (rule 8); 'undesirable' names that use an unconsented trademark, are purely descriptive, imply a foreign-government or regulated-financial connection, or are just a place name (rule 8A); and names containing words like Board, Commission, National, Union or Minister, which need prior Central Government approval before they can even be considered (rule 8B). Most first-time rejections are avoidable with a name search on the MCA and trademark databases first.

claim: Every person holding a DIN must file DIR-3 KYC once a year by 30 September for the preceding financial year. Missing the deadline deactivates the DIN on 1 October, blocking every MCA filing that director's signature is needed for, and reactivating it costs a flat ₹5,000 late fee per DIN regardless of how late it is. Common rejection causes are a name that doesn't match exactly across PAN, Aadhaar and the DIN record, address proof older than two months, or an oversized/non-compliant photo.

claim: A company must issue share certificates to the subscribers of the memorandum within 2 months of incorporation under section 56(4) of the Companies Act. Missing it draws a penalty of up to ₹50,000 on the company (₹25,000 for a small company) plus a matching penalty split across the officers in default, even when the delay is only a couple of weeks.

claim: A private limited company must maintain statutory registers from day one (register of members, register of directors and KMP, register of charges, minutes books for board and general meetings) even with a single meeting a year and no activity. Most founders never see this checklist until a due-diligence request or an ROC inspection asks for it, at which point reconstructing a year of minutes retroactively is the CA's problem to make look normal.

claim: A company current account can be opened through the bank option inside AGILE-PRO-S at incorporation, but the actual bank offered depends on which partner banks serve the registered office's location and pincode, so the founder does not always get their preferred bank. Founders who skip that option, or whose chosen bank isn't listed, do current-account KYC separately after incorporation with the Certificate of Incorporation, PAN, board resolution and director KYC documents, which commonly takes 1-2 weeks and stalls on address-proof or signature mismatches.

claim: Filing INC-20A even one day late still draws the full penalty: ₹50,000 on the company plus ₹1,000 per day of default on every officer in default, capped at ₹1 lakh per officer. Regulators have enforced this on delays as short as a single day, so 'I'll file it whenever' is not a safe plan even inside the 180-day window's shadow.

claim: Filing SPICe+ directly on the MCA portal without help avoids professional fees (just DSC ~₹1,000-2,000/director, name fee ₹1,000, and stamp duty), but requires comfort with a long web form, precise document formatting and enough patience for name and form rejections; a CA typically charges ₹3,000-25,000 on top of statutory fees to do it correctly, giving an assisted total around ₹12,000-30,000 for a simple two-director company. Online filing platforms advertise flat headline prices (₹1,999-7,999) that usually exclude government fees, stamp duty and DSC, and upsell those back in during the process.

claim: DIY founders most often lose time on name rejections from an unsearched name, mismatched details between PAN/Aadhaar/address proof, and picking an authorised capital or MoA object clause that doesn't fit the business, needing a later amendment. CA-assisted incorporations are more likely to go through cleanly but founders frequently discover after the fact that the CA used boilerplate MoA objects, a generic share structure with no vesting for co-founders, or an authorised capital padded to justify a higher fee. Cut-rate online platforms are the fastest to file but the least likely to explain what INC-20A, ADT-1 or the first AGM deadline actually mean, leaving the founder to discover the recurring obligations only when a penalty notice arrives.

claim: Closing a company that never took off is not free or instant: the fast-track exit (STK-2) government fee is ₹5,000 flat regardless of authorised capital, professional fees for a fully compliant company run ₹8,000-25,000 (much more, ₹25,000-75,000+, if annual filings were skipped and have to be caught up first), and the whole process from application to the name actually being struck off typically takes 3-6 months because of ROC processing and a mandatory public notice period.

claim: Fast-track strike-off requires the company to have nil assets and liabilities, all annual filings (AOC-4, MGT-7) up to date, GST cancelled if it was registered, valid DIR-3 KYC for every director, and final income tax returns filed — in other words, a founder cannot skip the paperwork on the way out either. A company that instead just goes dark and stops filing does not disappear: after three consecutive years of non-filing, every director is disqualified under section 164(2) from being a director of any Indian company for five years, and back-filing penalties can run to several lakh rupees before the ROC strikes it off anyway.
